commits.pr_title: [Docs] Warn that --api-key does not gate all endpoints
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

The `--api-key` boundary is currently only documented in `docs/usage/security.md`: it authenticates the `/v1`, `/v2`, and `/inference` path prefixes, but other endpoints on the same HTTP server — notably `/invocations`, which exposes the same inference capabilities as `/v1` — remain unauthenticated. Users (and LLM assistants, which frequently hit rate limits fetching the security docs) can easily miss this and expose an attacker-reachable inference surface.

This PR surfaces the same warning at the junctions where people actually look:

- **`vllm/entrypoints/openai/cli_args.py`** — expands the `--api-key` help text (rendered in `vllm serve --help` and the serve-args reference) to state the boundary and link to the security docs.
- **`docs/serving/online_serving/openai_compatible_server.md`** — adds a warning admonition separating `/v1` protections from unauthenticated endpoints like `/invocations`.

Both point to the [API Key Authentication Limitations](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security.html#api-key-authentication-limitations) section for the full list of protected/unprotected endpoints and recommended hardening.

This originated from a security researcher's suggestion that the warnings present in the security docs also appear in `--api-key`/`--help` text and in the main OpenAI-Compatible Server docs, so users have fewer opportunities to miss them.

## Not a duplicate

No open PR addresses documenting the `--api-key` authentication boundary in the CLI help text or the OpenAI-compatible server docs (checked `gh pr list --search "api-key invocations security docs"` and related keyword searches).

## Testing

Docs/help-text only; no runtime behavior changes.

- `pre-commit run --all-files` on the changed files (ruff, ruff-format, markdownlint, mypy, typos, etc.) — all passed.
- No model/accuracy/serving behavior is affected, so model evals are not applicable.

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft these documentation changes. The human submitter reviewed every changed line.

commits.pr_title: [Model] Add native Dots3 NOTE multimodal support
commits.pr_body:
## Motivation

Add native vLLM support for the complete Dots3 NOTE model, including:

- Text generation
- Image understanding
- Audio understanding
- Native video processing with interleaved visual and audio inputs
- FP8 MoE inference
- MTP speculative decoding
- OpenAI-compatible tool calling

Dots3 NOTE uses one unified Hugging Face model type and architecture:

- `model_type`: `dots3_note`
- `architectures`: `Dots3NoteForCausalLM`

The same architecture can serve the complete multimodal model or run only its language model through vLLM's existing `--language-model-only` option.

Dots3 NOTE's DSA layer is structurally related to DeepSeek-V3.2, but it cannot directly reuse the complete DeepSeek implementation because it combines:

- Full-attention MLA layers with DSA indexing
- Dense sliding-window MLA layers with different attention geometry
- Different attention gates for full-attention and SWA layers
- Different latent KV widths across attention layer groups
- A tail-RoPE DSA index-key checkpoint layout
- An SWA-shaped MTP layer
- A MoE vision encoder and an audio encoder
- Native video preprocessing that interleaves timestamped image and audio embeddings
- FP8 checkpoints whose dense dimensions may require TP-aware padding

## Model architecture

### Hybrid MLA attention

Dots3 NOTE alternates between two attention layer types.

Full-attention layers use:

- DeepSeek-style MLA
- DSA top-k indexing
- 128 attention heads
- A 512-dimensional latent KV representation
- A 64-dimensional RoPE component
- A model-specific attention gate
- Additional normalization on the RoPE-only index key

Sliding-window layers use:

- Dense sliding-window MLA
- 64 attention heads
- A 1024-dimensional latent KV representation
- 192 NoPE dimensions and 64 RoPE dimensions
- A 128-dimensional value head
- A bounded sliding window
- No DSA indexer

Because the two layer groups have different latent widths, MLA dimensions and KV-cache specifications must be derived from the actual attention layer rather than only from the top-level model configuration.

### DSA index and cache layout

The reused DeepSeek DSA implementation expects index keys in `[RoPE, NoPE]` order, while Dots3 NOTE checkpoints store them in `[NoPE, RoPE]` order.

Weight loading converts the relevant indexer tensors into the runtime layout:

- `wq_b.weight`
- `wk.weight`
- `k_norm.weight`
- `k_norm.bias`

The configuration also enables the GPT-J-style interleaved rotary layout used during NOTE training.

The DSA and SWA cache groups use different logical row widths:

- DSA: `512 + 64 = 576`
- SWA: `1024 + 64 = 1088`

Dots3 NOTE uses uniformly padded physical cache rows so the existing hybrid KV-cache allocator can manage both groups. A model-private sparse MLA implementation reads the logical DSA portion directly from the padded paged cache and adjusts physical block strides without flattening or cloning the complete cache pool.

### Sliding-window execution

Dots3 NOTE uses a private MLA specialization for SWA layers:

- Prefill uses expanded MHA and FlashAttention-3 varlen attention.
- Decode uses absorbed latent MQA over the paged sliding-window cache.
- Multi-token verification uses the same query-length-aware SWA path.
- Mixed batches preserve decode requests as decode requests and send only the prefill suffix through FA3.

The backend gathers only the required sliding-window region. Large prefill gathers are split according to the existing MLA workspace capacity instead of allocating a request-sized packed KV tensor.

For mixed batches, CPU sequence-length upper bounds are used only for workspace planning. Exact GPU sequence lengths rebuild the KV spans, sequence starts, token-to-request mapping, and cumulative sequence lengths before the gather is launched. This prevents the gather from reading blocks that have not been allocated or populated.

FA3 on Hopper does not directly support NOTE's `Q/K=256, V=128` combination through its different-head-dimension path. The model-private prefill backend pads V for the FA3 call and slices the result back to the logical 128-dimensional value representation.

### MoE and FP8 layout

Dots3 NOTE uses an ungrouped `noaux_tc` router. `Dots3NoteConfig` therefore defaults both `n_group` and `topk_group` to one instead of inheriting DeepSeek-V3's grouped-routing defaults, which would change expert selection.

The implementation supports NOTE's FP8 MoE checkpoint layout and reuses vLLM's existing fused MoE backends.

Shared-expert and dense MLP dimensions are padded only when required by both:

- The tensor-parallel world size
- The FP8 weight block size

The original logical dimensions and reduction semantics are preserved. The same padding rules are applied when loading dense MLP and MTP weights.

### MTP speculative decoding

`Dots3NoteMTP` is registered for vLLM speculative decoding.

It reuses the existing DeepSeek-V3.2 MTP orchestration and speculative-decoding interfaces while adapting:

- NOTE checkpoint names
- NOTE decoder-layer construction
- SWA attention geometry
- MTP embedding ownership
- Target LM-head sharing
- TP and FP8 dense-weight padding
- Multi-token SWA verification

The checkpoint-configured number of next-token prediction layers is preserved.

## Multimodal support

### Vision

The implementation includes the native Dots3 NOTE MoE vision transformer, vision attention, expert routing, projection, and image preprocessing.

Image inputs are converted into NOTE visual tokens and passed through the standard vLLM multimodal embedding interface.

### Audio

The implementation includes the native NOTE audio encoder and its configuration, convolutional frontend, transformer blocks, projection, and waveform preprocessing.

Audio is decoded and resampled through vLLM's multimodal frontend before being converted into NOTE audio embeddings.

### Video

Native video input is supported rather than requiring clients to manually extract frames.

The video processor:

- Decodes video frames
- Extracts the audio track when available
- Applies the model's context-dependent visual token budget
- Reserves output-token capacity
- Adds timestamps to sampled frames
- Interleaves visual frames and audio segments in temporal order
- Produces a single replacement span containing the corresponding multimodal embeddings

The video placeholder is aligned with the checkpoint tokenizer and chat template through `<|video_pad|>`.

Vision and audio towers are optional at runtime. `--language-model-only` skips their loading while retaining the same `Dots3NoteForCausalLM` architecture.

## Tool-calling support

This PR registers an opt-in `dots` tool-call parser for the OpenAI-compatible API.

The parser supports:

- Dots XML tool-call wrappers
- Multiple tool calls
- Multiple `invoke` elements within one wrapper
- Schema-aware parameter conversion
- JSON tool-call bodies as a fallback
- Streaming and non-streaming responses

Tool parsing is not enabled by default. Users can opt in with the existing vLLM tool-calling flags and `--tool-call-parser dots`.

## Shared vLLM changes

The shared changes are limited to general MLA capabilities required by hybrid MLA models.

### Per-layer MLA dimensions

The MLA metadata builder derives latent dimensions from the attention layer associated with each KV-cache group.

This allows hybrid MLA models to use different latent widths without changing existing single-layout MLA models.

### Sliding-window MLA cache specification

`MLAAttention` accepts an optional sliding window and emits a `SlidingWindowMLASpec` when configured.

This lets the standard hybrid KV-cache manager allocate bounded capacity for latent SWA caches.

### Explicit model-selected prefill backend

`MLAAttention` accepts an optional prefill backend class.

Dots3 NOTE uses this extension to select its private FA3 SWA prefill implementation without adding model-name checks or exposing a new user-selectable attention backend.

The PR no longer modifies the generic sparse-MLA flatten path, generic Triton decode kernel, or KV-cache zeroer.

## Parallelism

Dots3 NOTE integrates with existing vLLM parallel interfaces and supports:

- Tensor parallelism
- Pipeline parallelism
- Expert parallelism
- Data-parallel attention
- Sequence-parallel MoE
- MTP speculative decoding

Multimodal towers use vLLM's standard tower/language-model mapping and support language-model-only serving without introducing a separate model architecture.

## Validation

The implementation was validated with a Dots3 NOTE FP8 checkpoint on an 8-GPU Hopper system.

Validated paths include:

- Unified `Dots3NoteForCausalLM` configuration and registration
- FP8 checkpoint loading
- TP8 + EP8 service startup
- CUDA graph capture with `enforce_eager=False`
- OpenAI-compatible text generation
- Image input
- Audio input
- Native video input
- Full-attention DSA execution
- Sliding-window prefill and decode
- Mixed prefill/decode batches
- Multi-token SWA verification
- MTP checkpoint loading and generation
- Long-context chunked prefill
- Tool-parser unit tests
- Ruff, formatting, mypy, pre-commit, and DCO checks

The final FP8 Omni smoke test returned HTTP 200 for text, image, audio, and video requests. The service remained healthy without CUDA illegal-memory-access, OOM, or missing-weight errors.

commits.pr_title: Avoid long-blocking H2D copies in ViT
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose Two host-to-device copies on the per-iteration critical path can take a very long time to return. Despite `non_blocking=True`, the `cudaMemcpyAsync` call blocks the calling thread, and the time it takes tracks the amount of GPU work that has already been queued. That undoes the host run-ahead that asynchronous scheduling and CUDA graphs exist to build up. Neither call site looks suspicious at a glance, which is why this is easy to miss: **M-RoPE positions (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py`).** The staging buffer is pinned. However `mrope_positions` is allocated as `[3, max_num_tokens + 1]`, where the dummy trailing column is deliberately there to keep the tensor non-contiguous for `torch.compile`. That makes `cpu[:, :N]` a strided view of a pinned buffer. Using `CudaMemcpyAsync` with non-contiguous buffer leads to a silent synchronization. Copying the three rows individually — each row being contiguous within that same pinned allocation — makes the synchronization go away. Before M-RoPE fix: After M-RoPE fix: As shown above, the new three HtoDs became truly pinned and the synchronization goes away. There is still a very long `cudamemcpyasync` because we haven't fixed the following vision position ids copies yet. **Vision position ids (`vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_vl.py`).** `rot_pos_ids()` builds its per-image tensors from numpy, so the concatenated `pos_ids` is not pinned. Calling `.pin_memory()` before `.to(device, non_blocking=True)` makes the long copies go away. `pin_memory()` is a host-side copy only and does not change what is transferred. Before vision position ids fix: After vision position ids fix: After these two fixes, `cudaMemcpyAsync` synchronizations are totally eliminated. ## Scope The M-RoPE change affects models using M-RoPE (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL) on the V1 model runner. Model Runner V2 stages positions through UVA buffers and does not perform this copy, so it is unaffected. The vision position id change is specific to Qwen3-VL and is independent of the model runner. ## Test Plan Existing Qwen-VL correctness tests. The changes affect only how the transfer is issued, not what is transferred. ## Test Result Output is unchanged. Profiling shows the long-blocking copies are no longer present at either call site. ## What is measured, and what is not A microbenchmark that issues a single copy behind a fixed, deep queue of GPU work, sweeping only the copy size, shows a payload threshold. Below it the `cudaMemcpyAsync` call returns in microseconds. Above it the call takes roughly as long as the GPU work already queued, and stays at that cost as the payload grows further. Being explicit about the limits of that result: - The **root cause is not established.** We can show the threshold exists and is reproducible; we cannot yet say why. - The observation is that above the threshold **the call becomes very long**. We have not demonstrated that it is specifically a stream synchronization. - The threshold was found in a **microbenchmark**. It has not yet been confirmed end to end on a production model configuration. - We have not established what PyTorch does internally for a strided host source, so no claim is made about that path here. What is directly observable is the part this PR relies on: at both sites, issuing the transfer from pinned, contiguous memory removes the long-blocking copies. ---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Disable fine-grained prefix-cache hits for incompatible hybrid KV layouts
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Fine-grained prefix-cache hits are enabled for hybrid models containing Mamba `align` groups. However other groups, such as a sliding-window DSpark drafter, may use KV cache managers that only support block-aligned lookups. This previously caused an assertion when prefix caching was enabled.

This change:

- Enables fine-grained hits only when every KV cache manager supports the required lookup granularity.
- Falls back to scheduler-block-aligned prefix hits for incompatible layouts.
- Prevents the scheduler from creating partial-tail cache entries after that fallback.
- Keeps the drafter’s native sliding-window KV representation, avoiding model-specific overrides.
- Logs when fine-grained hits are disabled.

## Kimi K3 results with DSpark SWA 

- KV capacity is the same with and without: 7,815,323 tokens / 7.45× concurrency.
- Repeated 66,007-token prompt reused 57,600 tokens.
- The same hit remained after 300 GSM8K requests.
- Mean acceptance length: 4.87, 4.83, 4.83.
- GSM8K accuracy: 0.30, 0.32, 0.32.
- Zero invalid responses.

Short and medium prompts may receive no prefix-cache reuse because hits must land on the much larger scheduler alignment.

## Validation

- 23 partial-prefix-cache tests passed.
- 89 broader prefix-cache tests passed.
- Pre-commit passed.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Multimodal] Invalidate retained PyNvVideoCodec decoder after failure
commits.pr_body:
# Title

[Bugfix][Multimodal] Invalidate retained PyNvVideoCodec decoder after failure

# Body

Fixes #51138

## Summary

- invalidate a retained PyNvVideoCodec decoder slot when a borrowed operation
  exits with an error
- clear stale slot state before constructing a replacement decoder
- publish the replacement decoder only after construction succeeds
- add CPU-only regression coverage for borrow-time invalidation and failed
  replacement construction

## Root cause

PyNvVideoCodec reconfiguration is lazy. `SimpleDecoder.reconfigure_decoder()`
can return successfully before NVDEC parses the new stream's sequence header.
The actual capability check occurs when a later operation first parses or
decodes the reconfigured source.

For the reproduced failure, an unsupported 7680x4320 H.264 source selected a
native `NvDecoder` configured with maximum dimensions of 7680x4320. Its first
decode reached `NvDecoder::HandleVideoSequence`, where the GPU reported
4096x4096 maximum dimensions and a 65,536 macroblock limit. The 8K stream
requires 129,600 macroblocks, so `HandleVideoSequence` raised
`PyNvVCExceptionUnsupported` before decoder initialization completed.

That failed native decoder remained retained in `SimpleDecoder`'s internal
decoder cache with `max_width=7680` and `max_height=4320`. A subsequent clean
reconfiguration updated the demuxer and metadata correctly. Native callback
instrumentation confirmed that the next sequence callback received the clean
format (`coded=864x480`, `display=854x480`), not a replayed 8K sequence.
However, PyNvVideoCodec reused the same failed native `NvDecoder`, whose stored
maximum dimensions were still 7680x4320. The smaller clean source did not
reduce those retained maxima, and `HandleVideoSequence` compared them against
the GPU's 4096x4096 capability. The clean request therefore failed while still
reporting the stale 7680x4320 resolution.

The poisoned state is local to the retained decoder instance, not the source
metadata, CUDA stream, or CUDA context. Creating a new `SimpleDecoder` for the
same clean 480p source in the same process decoded successfully.

## Native RCA evidence

The failure was reproduced on an H200 NVL with PyNvVideoCodec 2.0.5 and NVIDIA
driver 595.71.05 using synthetic H.264/yuv420p inputs that differed only in
resolution:

| Step | Source / callback input | Retained native decoder state | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initial valid decode | coded 432x240, display 426x240 | max 432x240 | success |
| Unsupported decode | coded/display 7680x4320 | max 7680x4320; caps 4096x4096; MB cap 65,536 | fails: 129,600 MB unsupported |
| Clean decode after reconfigure | coded 864x480, display 854x480 | same native decoder; max still 7680x4320 | fails: retained resolution exceeds caps |
| Fresh clean decoder in same process | coded 864x480, display 854x480 | new native decoder | success, frame shape 480x854x3 |

Additional controls ruled out alternative explanations:

- valid-to-valid reconfiguration works, including replacing an intermediate
  source that was never decoded
- explicit CUDA synchronization and the default CUDA stream do not change the
  failure
- skipping the first valid decode does not change the failure
- disabling scanned stream metadata does not change the failure
- decoder cache size zero is coerced by PyNvVideoCodec to one; cache size one
  still reproduces the failure
- repeated clean reconfiguration and `seek_to_index(0)` do not recover the
  failed native decoder
- the Python wrapper's `stop()` calls a native method not exposed by the 2.0.5
  `SimpleDecoder`, so no supported reset operation is available

The exported `NvDecoder::HandleVideoSequence(CUVIDEOFORMAT*)` symbol was
instrumented to log both the callback format and the relevant native decoder
state. Disassembly of the installed binary independently confirmed that the
resolution error reads the retained decoder maximum dimensions rather than the
clean callback's coded dimensions.

NVIDIA's public Video Codec SDK sample follows the same high-level sequence:
`HandleVideoSequence` queries decoder capabilities and, for an initialized
session, performs hardware reconfiguration through `cuvidReconfigureDecoder`:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/video-sdk-samples/blob/master/Samples/NvCodec/NvDecoder/NvDecoder.cpp

## Why this fix is required

`_borrow_decoder_slot()` previously returned a slot to the retained vLLM pool
even when an operation inside the borrow raised. Because PyNvVideoCodec exposes
no reliable reset operation for this state, reconfiguring the same
`SimpleDecoder` cannot make the slot safe again.

Invalidation now runs whenever an exception escapes the borrowed-slot context.
The entire retained `SimpleDecoder`, including its internal native decoder
cache, is discarded. The next request therefore constructs a fresh decoder.
On a successful borrow, the slot returns to the pool with its decoder and
source path intact, so the existing reconfiguration path and its performance
benefit remain unchanged.

`_construct()` also clears stale slot state first and assigns the new decoder
only after `SimpleDecoder(...)` returns successfully. A replacement
construction failure therefore cannot republish either the old poisoned
decoder or a partial replacement.

## Upstream PyNvVideoCodec follow-up

This behavior should also be reported to the PyNvVideoCodec team. The vLLM
change remains necessary as a defensive resource-pool boundary, but the native
library should not retain or reuse a decoder session after
`HandleVideoSequence` fails during initialization.

Before filing upstream, the standalone reproducer should be rerun against the
latest public PyNvVideoCodec release (currently 2.1) to determine whether the
2.0.5 behavior is still present. If it reproduces, the report should include:

- PyNvVideoCodec, driver, CUDA, OS, Python, and GPU versions
- three synthetic inputs and their `ffprobe` output
- the minimal sequence: valid decode -> reconfigure to unsupported 8K and
  decode -> reconfigure to clean 480p and decode
- both exceptions, including native source locations and capability values
- evidence that the clean callback receives 864x480 while the error still
  reports retained 7680x4320
- confirmation that a fresh decoder succeeds in the same process
- controls for scanned metadata, CUDA stream synchronization, and cache size
- expected behavior: after a failed sequence initialization, either roll back
  the cached session, evict it, or mark it unusable so a later clean source
  creates a new native decoder

The NVIDIA Developer Forums category "Video Codec, PyNv & OFA" is the active
public reporting channel used by PyNvVideoCodec maintainers:
https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/c/gaming-and-visualization-technologies/video-processing-optical-flow/189

A separate compatibility issue can also be mentioned in the report: the Python
2.0.5 `SimpleDecoder.stop()` wrapper calls a native `stop` method that the
installed native `SimpleDecoder` does not expose.

## Duplicate-work check

Searches found no issue or pull request matching retained PyNvVideoCodec
decoder poisoning. Related decoder-pool PRs
[#44465](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44465) and
[#49753](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49753) do not fix
exception invalidation, so this change does not duplicate their work.

Open PR [#51120](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51120) is related
and complementary, not a duplicate. It changes unsupported or malformed
PyNvVideoCodec video exception mapping so selected native open failures become
`ValueError` and return HTTP 400. This branch protects retained decoder-pool
state after any exception escapes a borrowed slot. If #51120 merges first,
this branch should be rebased onto the resulting `video.py` and the focused
decoder-slot and media-error tests should be rerun before submission.

## AI-assistance disclosure

AI assistance was used to analyze the failure, implement and review the
focused change, run the documented validation workflow, and draft this pull
request.

## Test Plan

CPU-only transactional rebuild, generic invalidation, successful-retention,
and bounded-pool tests:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py::test_pynvvideocodec_failed_rebuild_invalidates_decoder_slot \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py::test_pynvvideocodec_borrow_error_invalidates_decoder_slot \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py::test_pynvvideocodec_decoder_slot_retains_simple_decoder \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py::test_pynvvideocodec_decoder_slots_are_bounded \
  -v
```

Result: `5 passed, 14 warnings`.

Focused PyNvVideoCodec decoder selection:

```bash
uv run --isolated --no-project \
  --with-requirements requirements/cpu.txt \
  --with pytest --with pytest-asyncio --with av --with tblib \
  python -m pytest tests/multimodal/test_video.py \
  -v -k "pynvvideocodec_decoder"

uv run --isolated --no-project \
  --with-requirements requirements/cpu.txt \
  --with pytest --with pytest-asyncio --with av --with tblib \
  python -m pytest \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py::test_pynvvideocodec_borrow_error_invalidates_decoder_slot \
  -v
```

Result: `4 passed, 61 deselected, 15 warnings`, plus
`1 passed, 15 warnings` for the regression omitted by the `-k` expression;
**5 focused tests passed, 0 failed**.

Wider multimodal selection on a non-CUDA host:

```bash
uv run --isolated --no-project \
  --with-requirements requirements/cpu.txt \
  --with pytest --with pytest-asyncio --with av --with tblib \
  python -m pytest \
  tests/multimodal/test_gpu_ipc_memory.py \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py \
  tests/multimodal/media/test_video.py \
  -q -k "gpu_memory or pynvvideocodec or hw_decoders"
```

Result: `19 passed, 2 skipped, 94 deselected, 15 warnings`. The two skips
are existing CUDA-required tests.

Ruff and whitespace checks:

```bash
.venv/bin/ruff check \
  vllm/multimodal/video.py tests/multimodal/test_video.py
.venv/bin/ruff format --check \
  vllm/multimodal/video.py tests/multimodal/test_video.py
git diff --check
```

Result: all checks passed; both files were already formatted and no
whitespace errors were found.

Pre-commit:

```bash
uvx --from 'pre-commit>=4.5.1' pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/multimodal/video.py \
  tests/multimodal/test_video.py
```

Result: all applicable hooks passed.

Diff scope:

```bash
git diff --check
git diff -- vllm/multimodal/video.py tests/multimodal/test_video.py

git diff --check \
  origin/main...HEAD

git diff --stat \
  origin/main...HEAD

git diff \
  origin/main...HEAD \
  -- vllm/multimodal/video.py tests/multimodal/test_video.py
```

Result: no whitespace errors; the committed patch contains only
`vllm/multimodal/video.py` and `tests/multimodal/test_video.py`
(`116 insertions, 1 deletion`).

## H200 integration validation

Ordered post-fix sequence:

```text
valid 240p before 8K:          HTTP 200
unsupported 8K:               HTTP 500, MBCount not supported (expected failure)
same valid 240p after 8K:      HTTP 200
different cache-busted 480p:  HTTP 200
health after:                  HTTP 200, ready
```

The unsupported input's HTTP error classification is outside this focused
change. This PR prevents that failed decode from poisoning later valid video
requests.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Return 400 for invalid PyNvVideoCodec video input
commits.pr_body:
## Summary
- translate `PyNvVideoCodec.PyNvVCException` raised while opening malformed video into a sanitized `ValueError`
- rely on vLLM's existing `ValueError` handler to return `BadRequestError`/HTTP 400 instead of HTTP 500
- preserve the native exception as the cause and leave unrelated decoder exceptions unchanged

## Root cause
A malformed user-supplied video reaches `PyNvVideoCodec.SimpleDecoder` during multimodal request preprocessing. The native `PyNvVCException` previously escaped the media boundary, so the generic API exception handler classified it as `InternalServerError`.

The same request returned the same HTTP 500 response through both the public NIM endpoint and the internal vLLM endpoint, and the traceback remained entirely in `vllm/multimodal/video.py` / PyNvVideoCodec before model inference.

- [x] Ruff lint and format checks
- [x] typos check
- [x] B200 end-to-end with vLLM 0.26.0 and PyNvVideoCodec backend:
  - corrupt MKV: HTTP 500 before, HTTP 400 after
  - valid MP4: HTTP 200
  - valid MKV: HTTP 200
  - four concurrent valid MP4 requests: all HTTP 200
  - health and basic text chat remain HTTP 200

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Fix MiniMax-M3 compressed-tensors FP8 MoE SwiGLU params
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

This PR fixes MiniMax-M3 accuracy when served from a compressed-tensors W8A8 FP8 MoE checkpoint.

MiniMax-M3 uses `hidden_act="swigluoai"` with non-default SwiGLU parameters:

- `swiglu_alpha=1.702`
- `swiglu_beta=1.0`
- `swiglu_limit=7.0`

The compressed-tensors FP8 MoE path already forwarded `swiglu_limit`, but did not forward `swiglu_alpha` or `swiglu_beta` into `make_fp8_moe_quant_config`. As a result, MiniMax-M3 compressed-tensors FP8 checkpoints could load and serve, but fused MoE used the wrong activation parameters and produced severely degraded outputs.

MiniMax-M3 exposed the issue because it combines compressed-tensors FP8 MoE with non-default SwiGLU-OAI parameters. Models using default SwiGLU behavior are unaffected because `None` preserves the existing default activation path.

This PR forwards:

- `gemm1_alpha=getattr(layer, "swiglu_alpha", None)`
- `gemm1_beta=getattr(layer, "swiglu_beta", None)`

from `CompressedTensorsW8A8Fp8MoEMethod.get_fused_moe_quant_config`.

It also adds a unit test covering the forwarding behavior.

## Test Result

End-to-end validation was run with a MiniMax-M3 compressed-tensors FP8 dynamic checkpoint served through vLLM.

Model:
https://huggingface.co/EmbeddedLLM/MiniMax-M3-FP8-dynamic

Before this fix, the checkpoint loaded and served, but quality was broken:

| Runtime | Model | Benchmark | Score |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| pre-fix vLLM | BF16 MiniMax-M3 | GSM8K strict EM | 95.30 |
| pre-fix vLLM | FP8 dynamic MiniMax-M3 | GSM8K strict EM | 0.00 |

After this fix, the same FP8 dynamic checkpoint recovered expected quality compared with BF16:

| Benchmark | BF16 MiniMax-M3 | FP8 dynamic MiniMax-M3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| GSM8K Platinum | 95.81 | 95.92 |
| GPQA Diamond | 77.78 | 77.95 |

commits.pr_title: [CI] Add registry layer cache to x86 CPU image build
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

The x86 CPU CI image build (`.buildkite/image_build/image_build_cpu.sh`) used
classic `docker build` with no layer cache, so every build recompiled
csrc/rust from scratch. This mirrors the registry-based BuildKit layer cache
already used for the CUDA CI image build (`image_build.sh`).

## What changed

- Switch from `docker build` + `docker push` to `docker buildx build --push`
  using a dedicated `vllm-cpu-builder` (`docker-container` driver, required
  for `type=registry` cache export).
- Add `prepare_cache_tags()` / `clean_docker_tag()`, ported from
  `image_build.sh`, resolving the same branch/PR/main fallback cache tags.
- Reuse the existing `vllm-ci-test-cache` / `vllm-ci-postmerge-cache` ECR
  repos, with every tag suffixed `-x86_cpu` so CPU cache blobs stay isolated
  from CUDA's (no new AWS infra needed).
- Add the private-ECR login needed to read/write those cache repos.
- `mode=max` on `--cache-to` so intermediate compile stages (rust-build,
  vllm-build, vllm-triton-cpu-build) are cached, not just the final image
  layer.

## Scope

- Only `.buildkite/image_build/image_build_cpu.sh` (the CI image build).
  `run-cpu-test.sh` (local test-runner build) is unchanged — it already
  benefits from the default BuildKit engine's local layer cache.
- `image_build_cpu_arm64.sh`, `image_build_hpu.sh`, `image_build_xpu.sh`,
  `image_build.yaml` are unchanged.

## Duplicate work

Searched open PRs/issues for CPU image-build caching; found none. The closest
related PR, #46711, adds registry caching to the x86 CUDA *release* image
builds and explicitly scopes CPU/ROCm as "unchanged" — this PR fills that gap
for the CI (non-release) CPU image build.

## Testing

- `bash -n .buildkite/image_build/image_build_cpu.sh`
- Traced `prepare_cache_tags()` for all four branch/PR scenarios (main
  postmerge, feature-branch push, PR into main, PR into a non-main branch)
  and confirmed the resolved `-x86_cpu`-suffixed tags match the intended
  fallback scheme.
- Local dry run against a scratch `registry:2` container (no AWS needed): a
  synthetic multi-stage Dockerfile was built once with `--cache-to
  type=registry,...,mode=max`, then rebuilt from a completely fresh builder
  using only `--cache-from` — every layer, including a simulated expensive
  compile stage, came back `CACHED`, confirming the cache round-trip works
  end-to-end.
- Opening as draft to let CI exercise the real ECR cache path on the actual
  CPU build queue before marking ready for review.

## Model evaluation

Not applicable — CI-only image build change, does not affect model output,
accuracy, or serving behavior.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][XPU] Run GDN attention as eager break under breakable cudagraph
commits.pr_body:
When breakable graph, Qwen3.5 on XPU produced garbage output. This PR is fix the GDN (Gated Delta Net) recurrent attention on XPU. 

The XPU GDN attention code reads and writes the conv and ssm state caches in place using data-dependent metadata. Under breakable-cudagraph capture the capture-time state addressing is frozen into the graph, so replay corrupts the recurrent state and hybrid models (e.g. Qwen3.5-9B) emit garbage output.

This PR wraps the gdn_attention_core_xpu custom op with eager_break_during_capture so it runs as an eager break during capture.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Reuse online NVFP4 MoE kernel across reloads
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Online NVFP4 MoE models re-run `process_weights_after_loading` whenever fresh BF16 weights are loaded and quantized in place. `_setup_kernel` currently also replaces the MoE kernel and quantization-config objects on every reload. Compiled and captured execution paths still reference the original kernel object, so replacing it can leave reloads executing against stale state and eventually produce non-finite outputs.

This change keeps the online NVFP4 MoE kernel and its quantization config stable for the lifetime of the layer. Weight conversion and `process_weights_after_loading` remain outside the guard and still run on every reload, so each fresh set of BF16 weights is quantized and installed as before.

Related to #41670 and #48902, but not a duplicate: this covers online NVFP4 and deliberately preserves per-reload weight processing.

AI assistance (OpenAI Codex) was used for investigation, implementation, and test drafting. I reviewed and understand the change.

## Test Plan

- Add a focused lifecycle test that calls `_setup_kernel` twice and verifies:
  - weight conversion runs twice;
  - processed weights are installed twice;
  - the MoE kernel is constructed once;
  - the quantization config is constructed once.
- Run formatting and lint checks on the changed files.
- Run paired five-step Prime-RL jobs with online NVFP4, piecewise CUDA graphs, two ETP=4 inference replicas, and a BF16 trainer. The jobs differ only by this fix.

## Test Result

- `uvx ruff check tests/quantization/test_online.py vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/nvfp4.py`: passed.
- `uvx ruff format --check tests/quantization/test_online.py vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/nvfp4.py`: passed.
- Focused lifecycle check in the deployment environment: two conversions, two weight-processing calls, one kernel construction, and one quantization-config construction.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Avoid repeated layerwise reload warning scans
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Avoid repeatedly scanning all concurrently buffered layerwise-reload state for every incoming weight tensor.

The overlap warning is now evaluated only when a layer first enters `LOADING_LAYERS`, and its detailed size/name calculation runs only when the set first transitions from one loading layer to two.

Related to #48312.

## Problem

`online_process_loader` runs once for every weight or packed shard applied during an online reload. When the loaded tensor is on an accelerator, the existing code does the following on every call:

1. adds the owning layer to `LOADING_LAYERS` (usually an idempotent add);
2. sorts the class names of all loading layers;
3. calls `get_info_size` for every loading layer, which walks its retained loaded-weight arguments;
4. invokes `logger.warning_once` with the current memory total and layer-name list.

The expensive work therefore repeats even when the set of loading layers did not change. In addition, the memory total grows as more weights arrive, so the arguments passed to `warning_once` change. Its cache consequently sees distinct keys instead of suppressing the repeated warning.

Large MoE reloads amplify this sharply: tens of thousands of weight applications repeatedly walk a growing collection of buffered weights and produce a warning/logging storm.

## Change

The warning block now requires that the layer is not already present in `LOADING_LAYERS`. After adding the new layer, it emits the detailed warning only when the set size is exactly two.

This preserves the useful signal—the first time multiple layers are buffered concurrently—while removing repeated work for later weights and later overlapping layers.

`LOADING_LAYERS` is explicitly logging-only state. Reload accounting, loader calls, materialization, post-load processing, copy-back, and the points where layers are removed or the set is cleared are unchanged.

## Validation

### Regression test

Added `test_layerwise_loading_warning_only_checks_new_layers`, which partially loads two layers several times and verifies that:

- detailed size accounting visits the two layers exactly once;
- the overlap warning is emitted once.

Red/green result in the vLLM CUDA container:

- unpatched `main`: **1 failed**;
- patched branch: **1 passed**.

Command equivalent:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py \
  -k layerwise_loading_warning_only_checks_new_layers -q
```

### Pre-commit

```bash
pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/model_executor/model_loader/reload/layerwise.py \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py
```

All applicable hooks passed, including Ruff check/format, mypy, SPDX, forbidden-import checks, and the signed-off-commit check.

### H200 end-to-end reload

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B INT4 was tested on eight H200 GPUs with the same existing runtime configuration on both sides:

- vLLM v0.25.1 compatibility baseline plus this change only;
- trainer TP1/PP4 on GPUs 0–3;
- two non-colocated rollout engines, TP2 each, on GPUs 4–7;
- explicit Triton WNA16 backend;
- 512 MiB packed weight-transfer buckets;
- no DIRECT or RUNTIME_VIEW reload fast path.

| Metric | Before | With this change |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial end-to-end weight update | 6075.7 s | **33.7 s** |
| Overlap allocation warnings | 179,828 | **2** |

The Ray job completed successfully. This is approximately a **180x** speedup for the affected reload and a **99.45%** reduction in elapsed time. The existing `MRotaryEmbedding` fallback warning remained unchanged and is outside this PR.

No model-output evaluation was added because this changes logging-only bookkeeping and does not modify tensors or inference execution.

## Duplicate-work check

I searched open vLLM PRs for `layerwise reload warning`, `LOADING_LAYERS`, and `weight reload performance warning`. No open PR addresses this repeated accounting/warning scan. The current reload lifecycle and graph-storage PRs cover different correctness and ownership concerns.

## AI assistance

commits.pr_title: [Frontend] Make `model` optional on all `/derender` request classes
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Makes `model` optional on all four `/derender` request classes — `DerenderChatRequest`, `DerenderCompletionRequest`, `DerenderChatStreamRequest`, `DerenderCompletionStreamRequest` — and resolves the served model name server-side via `request.model or self.models.model_name()` when the field is omitted.

Every comparable endpoint already treats `model` as optional:

| Endpoint | `model` |
| --- | --- |
| `/tokenize`, `/detokenize` | `str \| None = None` (`serve/tokenize/protocol.py:25,51,167`) |
| `/v1/chat/completions/render`, `/v1/completions/render` | `str \| None = None` (takes `ChatCompletionRequest` / `CompletionRequest` directly) |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions` | `str \| None = None` |
| `GenerateRequest` | `str \| None = None` |
| **`/derender` (before this PR)** | **`model: str` — required** |

### Why it was required, and why that doesn't hold up

`/derender` is the only endpoint in this family that builds a *final* OpenAI response object, and both `ChatCompletionResponse.model` (`openai/chat_completion/protocol.py:130`) and `CompletionResponse.model` (`openai/completion/protocol.py:627`) declare `model` as a required `str`. `request.model` was derender's only source for that field. Tokenize returns `TokenizeResponse` and render returns `GenerateRequest`; neither carries a model name, so neither had a forcing function.

But `/v1/chat/completions` never echoes `request.model` into its response — it resolves the name server-side (`openai/chat_completion/serving.py:268`):

```python
model_name = self.models.model_name(lora_request)
```

`ServingDerender` extends `BaseServing`, which already assigns `self.models` (`serve/engine/serving.py:36`), so the same resolver was available with no new plumbing.

### Validation is unchanged

`_is_model_supported` (`serve/engine/serving.py:70-75`) already short-circuits on a falsy name, so omitting `model` makes `_check_model` a no-op — matching tokenize's existing behavior. A **wrong** model name is truthy, so it never reaches that short-circuit and still 404s:

| `model` in body | Result |
| --- | --- |
| omitted (`None`) | validation skipped; response carries `self.models.model_name()` |
| `"does-not-exist"` | **404 `NotFoundError`, `param="model"` — unchanged** |
| valid served name or LoRA name | 200, echoed back |

`test_derender_chat_unknown_model` covers that 404 and still passes.

One behavior change worth naming explicitly: `{"model": ""}` previously echoed `model: ""` and now returns the served name, because `"" or X` is `X`. This matches what `/v1/chat/completions` already does for the same input (pinned by `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py:874`), so it is a convergence rather than a regression — but it is not byte-identical.

### Design notes

- The fallback lives in the serving layer, **not** as a pydantic validator or field default. `_check_model` reads `request.model` off the request object (`serve/engine/serving.py:40-47`), so defaulting at parse time would make validation inspect a server-invented name and erase the "client said nothing" vs "client said this" distinction.
- `request.model` is still preferred when supplied, rather than always recomputing as chat completions does. This keeps existing callers' responses unchanged, including any passing a LoRA adapter name.
- `vllm/renderers/online_derenderer.py` is **unmodified** — its `model: str` parameters stay required and receive the already-resolved value.
- `docs/serving/online_serving/derenderer.md:42,50` includes these classes via `--8<--` snippet markers, so the published request format regenerates with no docs edit.

## Why this is not a duplicate

```
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "derender"
```

Returns #50550, #47931, #49876, #45521, #47438. None makes `model` optional (#49876 is an Inkling parser fix and #47438 an OpenCUA processor fix; they surfaced in the text search only). The one real overlap is **#50550** (stream reasoning and tool calls from the derender endpoint), which edits the same two streaming methods in `serving.py` — but this diff adds only two lines per method there, and leaves `online_derenderer.py` (where #50550 does its work) untouched. Whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase.

## Why this is not busywork

In the disaggregated `render → generate → derender` pipeline, every caller had to thread a redundant `model` through a request that otherwise carries no model-identifying information — it operates purely on token IDs returned by a prior `/render` plus `/inference/v1/generate` round trip — even though the derender service already knows which model it serves.

## Test commands and results

All runs on the final tree (`4b0f96a0a9`). Note `.venv/bin` must be on `PATH` or the server fixture fails to find the `vllm` CLI.

**Derender suite:**
```
python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/ -q
→ 57 passed, 16 warnings, 14 errors in 71.77s
```

The 14 errors are pre-existing and environmental, not caused by this change. They are `ERROR at setup` — the test bodies never run — in `test_e2e_*` / `test_parity_*`, which use separate module-scoped server fixtures for `PARSER_MODEL` (`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B`) and `openai/gpt-oss-20b`. Root cause:

```
huggingface_hub.errors.FileMetadataError: Distant resource does not seem to be on
huggingface.co. It is possible that a configuration issue prevents you from
downloading resources from https://huggingface.co.
```

The weights are cached locally; it is revision-metadata resolution over the network that fails in this sandbox. A change to pydantic field types plus four lines of name resolution cannot cause an HTTP metadata lookup to fail. **Reviewers with network access should confirm these 14 pass in CI.**

**New test:**
```
python -m pytest tests/.../test_derender.py::test_derender_chat_model_omitted_resolves_served_name -v
→ 1 passed
```
Asserts the resolved *value* (`response.json()["model"] == MODEL_NAME`), not merely a 200, so it proves the fallback fired.

**Wrong-model guard still fires:**
```
python -m pytest tests/.../test_derender.py::test_derender_chat_unknown_model -v
→ 1 passed  (404 preserved)
```

**Sibling render suite** — shares the `_check_model` path:
```
python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/scale_out/render/ -v
→ 26 passed, 2 errors (pre-existing Qwen3-VL config fetch, same network cause)
```
`test_completion_render_error_invalid_model` and `test_chat_completion_render_error_invalid_model` both PASSED.

**Empty-string regression guard** — this change deliberately does not touch `_is_model_supported`:
```
python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py::test_serving_chat_returns_correct_model_name -v
→ 1 passed in 3.59s
```

**Lint and types**, scoped to the three changed files:
```
pre-commit run --files vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/protocol.py \
  vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/serving.py \
  tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/test_derender.py
→ ruff check Passed, mypy Passed, SPDX Passed, forbidden-imports Passed; zero files modified
```

### Test scope, stated plainly

One test was added, covering the chat non-streaming endpoint. The other three edits are identical copies of the same one-line resolution and are exercised by the existing suite's happy paths, which pass `model` explicitly. A reviewer who wants the omitted-`model` path covered on the streaming endpoints could add it cheaply against the existing `MagicMock` harness at `tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/test_derender_stream.py:456` — no server needed. Flagging it rather than leaving it to be discovered.

## Model evaluation

None run, and none applicable. This change affects only the `model` metadata field on the response envelope. It does not touch tokenization, sampling, prompt construction, or output parsing — `online_derenderer.py`, where all detokenization and reasoning/tool-call parsing lives, is byte-for-byte unmodified. There is no path by which it can alter generated text, so there is nothing for an eval to measure.

## AI assistance

Per `AGENTS.md`: **AI assistance was used.** This change was authored with Claude Opus 5 under human direction — design, implementation, and review were driven through an agent workflow, and the test and lint commands quoted above were executed in that session, with their real output reproduced here rather than summarized.

The change is deliberately small and auditable for human verification: 3 files, +37/−14, and the production delta is four field-type changes plus one resolution line per method. The submitting human is responsible for reviewing every changed line and confirming the results above before this leaves draft status.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][V1][Multimodal] Recover from P0/P1 processor cache drift (#46747)
commits.pr_body:
Summary:

## Purpose

The multi-modal IPC processor cache keeps two copies that are assumed to stay mirrored: a metadata-only "shadow" on P0 (the API / front-end process) and the real tensor cache on P1 (the engine process). On a P0 shadow hit, P0 forwards `data=None` and trusts that P1 still holds the item. Because the two processes update their byte-budgeted LRU caches in different orders — P0 processes multi-modal items concurrently while P1 ingests them serially — the caches can drift apart, leaving P0 referencing an item that P1 has already evicted. When that happens, `MultiModalReceiverCache.get_and_update_item` on P1 hits `assert mm_item is not None` and the request fails unrecoverably. A client that re-sends previously cached items by hash only (no data) after an idle gap can surface a whole batch of drifted hashes at once.

The mirrored-eviction invariant documented on `BaseMultiModalCache` — P0 and P1 stay in lock-step, so P1 membership can be inferred from P0 without an extra IPC round-trip — cannot be guaranteed across a concurrent, separate-process front-end, so a drift should be recoverable rather than fatal.

This PR makes the drift self-heal on the first retry, entirely server-side:

- `MultiModalReceiverCache.get_and_update_item` raises a typed `MultiModalCacheMissError` (carrying the `mm_hash`) instead of asserting when an item arrives with no data and is not cached on P1. `get_and_update_features` collects every drifted hash in a request and raises once, so a single retry recovers the whole request instead of one round-trip per item.
- `EngineCore.process_input_sockets` catches it and returns a retryable response carrying the missing hashes via a new `EngineCoreOutput.mm_cache_miss_hashes` field. The field is appended last so the `array_like` positional serialization stays backward compatible, and because `EngineCoreOutput` sets `omit_defaults=True` it is omitted from the wire entirely unless a drift occurs.
- `AsyncLLM`'s output handler drops those hashes from the P0 sender cache via a new `BaseMultiModalProcessorCache.invalidate(mm_hash)`, so the client's resend (now with data) takes the cache-miss path on P0 and repopulates P1.

The happy path is unchanged: a P0/P1 cache hit still returns early, before any of the new code runs, so there is no steady-state latency cost.

Test Plan:
## Test Plan

New CPU-only unit tests in `tests/multimodal/test_cache.py` — they build the caches from a stub model config, so they need no Hugging Face download or network access:

- `test_mm_cache_miss_raises_and_recovers` — the P1 receiver raises `MultiModalCacheMissError` (carrying the hash) on a miss-with-no-data; `MultiModalProcessorSenderCache.invalidate()` drops the stale shadow entry; and the full round-trip recovers (invalidate -> resend with data -> P1 repopulated -> a subsequent hash-only request succeeds).
- `test_mm_cache_miss_batches_all_drifted_hashes` — when several items in one request are drifted, `get_and_update_features` collects every missing hash and raises once, so a single retry recovers the whole request; non-drifted items in the same request are still ingested.

```
pytest tests/multimodal/test_cache.py -k mm_cache_miss
```

## Test Result

The two new tests are deterministic CPU-only tests (no GPU/network) and run in CI via `pytest`; the rest of `tests/multimodal/test_cache.py` is unaffected. The underlying fix has also been exercised under sustained real-world multimodal (image) serving traffic: the engine recovered from P0/P1 cache drift on retry, with no `assert mm_item is not None` crashes and no engine restarts.

## Purpose
Kimi's KDA layers do three things per decode step for every sequence and every value head:

1. Causal conv1d update over the Q/K/V projections, advancing a small per-sequence convolution state
2. Gated delta-rule recurrence, which updates a `[head_dim, head_dim]` recurrent state and produces the attention output
3. gated RMSNorm on that output

On ROCm, currently these run as separate Triton kernels. This PR mirrors the CUDA path, adds a HIP equivalent of the fusion kernel for single-token decode steps. It shows speedup compared with separate Triton kernel launches, and shows improvement to output throughput by ~7% in e2e benchmark.

## Summary

`_quantize_pad_fp8_kernel` in `vllm/kernels/triton/qkv_padded_fp8_quant.py` fails to compile under `torch.compile` when the ViT encoder is compiled with FP8 encoder attention (`compile_mm_encoder`), because its `fp8_min` / `fp8_max` scalar arguments are typed as `fp64` by Inductor. This PR declares them `tl.constexpr` so the kernel composes with `torch.compile`.

## Error

When the FP8 ViT encoder attention path is compiled, the `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM` pass rejects the FP8 conversion during Triton's `make_llir` stage:

```
Unsupported conversion from f64 to f8E4M3FN with rounding mode rtne
LLVM ERROR: Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.
error: Failures have been detected while processing an MLIR pass pipeline
note: Pipeline failed while executing [`ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM` on 'builtin.module' operation]
```

Triton raises this as `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed`, which Inductor then wraps as:

```
InductorError: Failed to run autotuning code block
```

The kernel signature metadata captured at failure time shows the two scalar bounds typed as `fp64`:

```
'signature': { ... 'fp8_min': 'fp64', 'fp8_max': 'fp64', ... }
```

The failing IR op is the FP8 cast itself:

```
%6 = tt.fp_to_fp %3, rounding = rtne : tensor<...xf64> -> tensor<...xf8E4M3FN>
```

## Root cause

`fp8_min` and `fp8_max` are Python floats passed into the Triton kernel, and eager Triton and Inductor type them differently. An eager Triton launch types a Python `float` argument as `fp32` (`triton/runtime/jit.py`), whereas Inductor / `torch.compile` types a Python `float` argument as `fp64` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/triton_utils.py` — "Python floats are natively fp64, so use fp64 to preserve precision").

Inside the kernel the bounds feed a clamp immediately before the FP8 cast:

```python
x_q = tl.clamp(x_q, fp8_min, fp8_max).to(y_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
```

With `fp64` bounds, `tl.clamp(fp32_tensor, fp64, fp64)` promotes `x_q` to `fp64`, so the final cast becomes `fp64 -> fp8e4nv` (`tt.fp_to_fp` from `f64` to `f8E4M3FN` with `rtne` rounding). Triton's NVIDIA backend has no lowering for that conversion — `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM` errors with `Unsupported conversion from f64 to f8E4M3FN with rounding mode rtne` and `make_llir` fails (`PassManager::run failed`), which Inductor then wraps as the autotuning error above. The kernel runs fine in eager mode, where Triton types the same bounds as `fp32` so the clamp and cast stay `fp32 -> fp8e4nv`; only the `torch.compile` path types them as `fp64` and hits the missing lowering. The failure therefore went unnoticed until the FP8 ViT encoder attention path was compiled via `compile_mm_encoder`.

## Fix

`fp8_min` / `fp8_max` are compile-time constants (`_FP8_MIN` / `_FP8_MAX`, from `get_fp8_min_max()`). Declaring them `tl.constexpr` bakes them into the kernel as fp32-behaving literals, so no runtime float scalar exists for Inductor to type as `fp64`, the clamp stays `fp32`, and the kernel composes with `torch.compile`.

## Purpose

Continue the test-only follow-up identified in #51275 by removing probe-then-bind TCP rendezvous from two single-node distributed test launchers.

- switches the DCP A2A multiprocessing launcher to one unique `file://` rendezvous shared by its local workers;
- switches the CUDA Async-TP spawn test to an explicit FileStore init method and rank/world-size arguments;
- adds focused coverage that FileStore init methods are unique.

commits.pr_title: [Hardware][AMD] Enable fused bf16→fp32 router GEMM on ROCm
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

This pull request addresses issue #50267 by enabling fused bf16→fp32 GEMM operations on AMD ROCm hardware for MoE router gates.

## Problem Statement

The MoE router gate requires `out_dtype=torch.float32` for the `grouped_topk` operation. However, on ROCm, the fused fp32-output GEMM implementation was gated exclusively to CUDA platforms. This caused a fallback to bf16 GEMM followed by a separate cast operation, creating a standalone "bf16→fp32 copy kernel" visible in performance traces between the router GEMM and `grouped_topk` for every MoE layer on each decode step.

## Solution

The changes enable hipBLASLt's `out_dtype` epilogue support (analogous to CUDA's cuBLAS capability) by modifying `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py`:

- Adds ROCm as an alternative condition for `allow_cublas_router_gemm` when: no bias exists, weights are bf16, and output is fp32
- Updates both `__init__` and `set_out_dtype` methods to ensure consistency
- The fused tier now executes on ROCm, folding the fp32 cast into the GEMM epilogue

## Impact Assessment

**CUDA:** No changes; the condition uses `current_platform.is_rocm()`, which evaluates false on CUDA.

**Correctness:** Verified on gfx942 hardware; results match fp32 reference within ~6e-5 tolerance.

**Scope:** Router gate only; expert GEMMs and other fp32 operations remain unaffected.

## Performance Results

Benchmarked on ROCm (gfx942) using the online serving benchmark: baseline vs. fused, 3 seeds each (123 / 456 / 789), max concurrency 4, 40 requests per run (40960 input + 40960 generated tokens). All runs completed 40/40 successful with 0 failures.

Averaged across the 3 seeds:

| Metric                    | Baseline | Fused (this PR) | Δ              |
|---------------------------|----------|-----------------|----------------|
| Benchmark duration (s)    | 343.18   | 337.69          | −5.5 s (−1.6%) |
| Output throughput (tok/s) | 119.35   | 121.29          | +1.9 (+1.6%)   |
| Total throughput (tok/s)  | 238.71   | 242.59          | +3.9 (+1.6%)   |
| Mean TPOT (ms)            | 32.87    | 32.34           | −0.53 (−1.6%)  |
| Mean ITL (ms)             | 32.87    | 32.34           | −0.53 (−1.6%)  |
| Mean TTFT (ms)            | 689.65   | 688.97          | ≈flat (−0.1%)  |

**Interpretation:** Folding the fp32 cast into the router GEMM epilogue removes a per-MoE-layer, per-decode-step conversion kernel from the critical path. The decode-path metrics (TPOT, ITL, output throughput) all improve by a consistent ~1.6%, while TTFT is unchanged as expected since prefill is not dominated by that per-step kernel. Variance across seeds is small (throughput within ±0.2 tok/s, TPOT within ±0.07 ms), so the improvement is stable and above noise, if modest.

## Testing Plan

- Confirm the standalone `bfloat16tofloat32_copy_kernel` is absent from ROCm traces
- Validate router logits match previous behavior within tolerance
- Unit tests added for the modification

commits.pr_title: [Perf] Avoid more GPU<->CPU syncs on the model execution path
commits.pr_body:
Follow-on to the earlier sync-avoidance work, splitting further fixes out of the VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK branch. Each of these removes a host roundtrip rather than suppressing it:

- kv-sharing fast prefill: derive the fast-prefill decode metadata from host-side data. `total_num_decode_tokens` is just the number of logits indices, and the max per-request logits count is plumbed down from the runner (which already has it on the host as `num_sampled_tokens`) via a new `CommonAttentionMetadata.max_logits_per_req`, replacing a `.max().item()` / `.sum().item()` pair per step.
- mamba2: derive `prep_initial_states` from the CPU prefill metadata instead of `torch.any(has_initial_states_p).item()`. Factored the shared derivation out of `_build_chunk_metadata_tensors` as `_prefill_cpu_metadata`.
- EPLB: `_pad_out_tensor` was missing `non_blocking=True`, so the commit of the logical map blocked the async worker thread.
- gemma4: cache a per-device suppressed-token index tensor and use `index_fill_`, instead of list-indexing with a Python scalar per call.
- diffusion_gemma: take a device tensor in `init_canvas` and hoist the slot-index transfer; use `fill_()` for 1-D scalar stores.
- glm4_1v / phi4mm: `async_tensor_h2d` instead of `torch.tensor(..., device=)`, and `.bool()` instead of a `.type(torch.BoolTensor)` host roundtrip.
- multimodal processors (internvl, interns1, phi3v, step3_vl, keye, audioflamingo3): mark token-id and size fields `keep_on_cpu=True` so they are not staged to device only to be read straight back.

These were extracted from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43107.

Claude code was used to help with this.

commits.pr_title: [CI] Stabilize tensor IPC multiprocessing tests
commits.pr_body:
- Use an explicit spawn context for all queues, events, barriers, and worker processes without changing the process-wide multiprocessing default.
- Give spawned workers one shared 60-second startup and result deadline to accommodate slower ROCm imports.
- Tag encoder and decoder results by role instead of assuming cross-process queue ordering.
- Preserve the shorter tensor transport timeouts so a real IPC stall still fails promptly.
- Always release workers and perform bounded join, terminate, and kill cleanup when a test fails or times out.

PR #32104 introduced short parent deadlines and incomplete failure cleanup into this test harness. On ROCm, the parent timed out while children were still importing, then destroyed synchronization objects and produced misleading `SemLock` errors in the [engine test step](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11570/list?sid=019fc12a-ba41-42f0-94ac-bd219748b386&tab=output). The test remains spawn-based, matching vLLM's `torch_shm` requirement and PyTorch accelerator-sharing constraints. All 12 tensor IPC tests pass locally after the harness changes.

## Purpose

This PR enables DeepSeek-V4 checkpoints on ROCm gfx11/RDNA devices.

It removes Python-side blockers in the ROCm sparse-indexer path and allows DeepSeek-V4 checkpoints mapped to `INCConfig` to pass ROCm platform validation:

- Register ROCm sparse-indexer ops on gfx11.
- Let `SparseAttnIndexer.forward_hip()` delegate to the ROCm sparse-indexer custom op and use the op-level fallback instead of failing early on platform capability checks.
- Add `inc` to `RocmPlatform.supported_quantization` so the checkpoint passes ROCm validation.

## Test Plan

The validation checkpoint is:

```text
Intel/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound
```

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=rocm \
PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx1100 \
python setup.py build_ext --inplace
```

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
```

## Summary

Enable FlashInfer XQA decode on SM120/SM121 through FlashInfer's dedicated XQA API.

- Select XQA for SM12x decode.
- Support uniform and ragged speculative decode through `q_len_per_req` and `q_cu_seq_lens`.
- Build the packed causal or non-causal draft mask required by XQA.
- Support sliding-window decode, attention sinks, non-causal draft attention, and uniform-batch CUDA graphs on SM12x.
- Keep the existing SM90 shared-XQA path and SM100 trtllm-gen path unchanged.
- Align the Python, cubin, JIT-cache, and Docker pins on FlashInfer 0.6.16.post1.

## Dependency

This PR requires [FlashInfer 0.6.16.post1](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/releases/tag/v0.6.16.post1), which includes the required upstream support from [flashinfer#4137](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4137) and [flashinfer#4199](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4199). commits.pr_title: [Profiler] Add minimal Triton Proton profiling backend

## Purpose

Add Triton Proton as an optional worker profiling backend alongside PyTorch and CUDA profiling. This first PR deliberately supports NVIDIA GPUs through CUPTI and graph-free execution only, keeping the core worker integration small and reviewable.

- Expose typed Proton context, data, CUPTI backend, output format, mode, and Triton hook configuration.
- Keep Proton lazily imported so other profiler users do not need a Proton-capable Triton installation.
- Finalize each profiling request independently with constructor-owned, per-request prefix-, rank-, process-, instance-, and run-qualified output names.
- Validate Proton data/output combinations only when Proton is selected, reject Proton-only options under other profilers, and gate newer capabilities on the installed Triton version.
- Skip annotation construction outside the active profiling window.
- Reject unsupported platforms during configuration validation with an actionable error.
- Require graph-free execution via either `--enforce-eager` or `cudagraph_mode=NONE`; CUDA graph attribution is isolated in #51084.

The implementation intentionally uses the common profiler lifecycle without Proton-specific start, stop, or shutdown overrides.

## Platform scope

This PR is intentionally NVIDIA/CUPTI-only. Correct ROCm support requires node-appropriate device-visibility propagation through both Ray executor implementations, which would substantially broaden this minimal integration. ROCm/`rocprofiler` support is deferred to a dedicated follow-up.

## Split follow-ups

- #51084 adds CUDA graph capture and replay attribution.
- #51085 adds distributed partial-start rollback, HTTP error mapping, generic profiler lifecycle recovery, and numeric trace metadata.

Both follow-ups depend only on this PR and are independent of each other. This keeps generic executor/API reliability and CUDA graph model-runner changes out of the initial backend integration.

Searched open vLLM PRs and issues for `Triton Proton` and `Proton profiler`; no duplicate implementation was found beyond this series.

Model/output impact: none. This changes profiling behavior only and does not alter model outputs, accuracy, or serving semantics.

The implementation uses vLLM's existing canonical Triton dependency. Explicit `hatchet` and `chrome_trace` output is supported by Triton 3.6; `hatchet_msgpack` and `periodic_flushing` require Triton 3.7 or newer. Unsupported configurations fail before session creation.

commits.pr_title: [4/N][KV-Cache Layout Refactor] Promote local KV cache specs via a class-changing replace helper
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`_promote_local_kv_cache_specs` rebuilds each promoted spec with a hand-written constructor call per class, and the explicit field lists have drifted: the MLA and chunked-local promotions silently drop `kv_quant_mode` (mis-sizing promoted pages for quantized KV caches), and the chunked-local promotion drops `head_size_v`.

This PR adds `replace_as()` — `dataclasses.replace` generalized to rebuild a spec as a different class — and drives the promotion from a source→target class mapping resolved through the MRO (the `functools.singledispatch` idiom, so subclasses hit their own entry first). Every shared field is carried automatically; new spec fields can no longer be silently lost in promotion.

Behavior changes (both bug fixes):
- Promoted MLA and chunked-local specs now retain `kv_quant_mode`.
- Promoted `SlidingWindowMLASpec` records its `sliding_window`, matching what the `SlidingWindowSpec` promotion already does per the `FullAttentionSpec` docstring ("we use FullAttentionSpec and record the sliding window size").

Extracted from the KV-layout standardization work (#44458 / RFC #42082) since it stands alone.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Give KV-first attention blocks their own page in hybrid models
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

On MI300, DSpark speculative decoding on `RedHatAI/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` produces garbage for most requests in a batch. GSM8K accuracy drops to 0.20 against 0.95 for the same target model without speculation, and `test_dspark_correctness_and_acceptance_rate[qwen3.6-speculators]` fails. The same test passes on H200.

Hybrid models share a single page pool between the full-attention layers, the Mamba/GDN state layers, and the draft model's layers. That sharing is only safe because every group agrees that block id `b` occupies page `b`, i.e. the bytes `[b * page_size, (b + 1) * page_size)`.

ROCm's KV cache layout breaks that agreement. Its shape is `(2, num_blocks, block_size, num_kv_heads, head_size)`, so K and V live in two far-apart halves of the allocation and block `b` actually covers half of page `b / 2` plus half of page `num_blocks / 2 + b / 2`. Attention blocks and Mamba state pages therefore resolve to overlapping bytes and scribble over each other. Backends whose block dimension comes first, such as `TRITON_ATTN` and the NVIDIA paths, keep the agreement and are unaffected, which is why this is ROCm-only.

The corruption is silent. Instrumenting the first full-attention layer showed clean inputs and `NaN` outputs for two of four sequences, with `NaN` values sitting inside the valid context range of those sequences' KV cache blocks. The affected sequences were exactly the ones holding an even block id, matching the factor of two between the layout and the page size. A single `NaN` key poisons the whole softmax row, so the target returns degenerate logits and the decoded text collapses.

The fix builds the view page-first, then swaps the dimensions back, so each block owns exactly its own page. It applies only to KV-first attention layers whose allocation is also used by Mamba state; blocks-first backends and attention-only allocations keep their current layout. The logical shape is unchanged, so kernels see exactly what they saw before.

## Test Plan

Unless noted, everything below ran on a single MI300 (gfx942) with `RedHatAI/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` plus `RedHatAI/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-speculator.dspark`.

1. The originally failing case:
   `pytest "tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dspark/test_dspark.py::test_dspark_correctness_and_acceptance_rate[qwen3.6-speculators]"`
2. The whole file, to cover the other speculator/model combinations:
   `pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dspark/test_dspark.py`
3. KV cache layout unit tests:
   `pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py tests/v1/core/test_contiguous_kv_packing.py`
4. A 40-question greedy GSM8K run with speculation on the default ROCm backend, before and after the change.
5. Two new unit tests in `tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py`: one asserts that a KV-first layer sharing its allocation with Mamba gives every block its own page, the other asserts that an attention-only allocation keeps the existing layout.

## Test Result

1. Passes. It failed before the change.
2. All three cases pass.
3. 94 passed.
4. GSM8K accuracy goes from 0.200 to 0.900 with no invalid answers, and the mean accepted length goes from about 1.0 to 5.36 tokens, so speculation is doing real work instead of having every draft rejected. For reference, the same model without speculation scores 0.950, and forcing `TRITON_ATTN` on both target and draft scored 0.925.
5. Both pass with the change. The first one fails without it, the control passes either way.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][MoE] Fix expert_map vs AITER expert_mask for non-AITER experts under EP
commits.pr_body:
`RoutedExperts.expert_map` returned the AITER 0/1 `expert_mask` whenever AITER
fused MoE is enabled (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`), regardless of which experts
kernel actually runs. Non-AITER kernels (Triton `moe_wna16`, MXFP4 emulation,
Marlin, …) expect the canonical global→local `expert_map` (`-1` for non-local)
and misread the 0/1 mask as slot indices → every token collapses onto local
slot 0/1 → garbage under EP.

Fix: `RoutedExperts.expert_map` asks the resolved experts kernel which
representation it consumes. Only the AITER CK kernels — `AiterExperts` (via
`rocm_aiter_fused_experts`) and `AiterMxfp8Experts` — set `consumes_expert_mask`
and receive the precomputed 0/1 `expert_mask`; every other kernel gets the
canonical `_expert_map`. This keys on the actual per-layer kernel rather than
the global `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER` switch (which does not reflect the kernel a
WNA16 / Marlin / emulation layer ends up on). The AITER experts forward the
precomputed mask to aiter unchanged — no per-forward derive — and quark's
non-modular path passes `layer.expert_mask` directly. `expert_mask` stays a
live buffer; every quant method keeps passing `layer.expert_map` unchanged.

**Accuracy** (Kimi-K2.6 INT4 / compressed-tensors WNA16, MI350X gfx950, TP4):
plain `--enable-expert-parallel` gsm8k 5-shot **0.00 → 0.95**; DP2×TP4 EP via
`mori_high_throughput` (modular kernel) **0.925/0.955**. The mask handed to the
AITER kernels is byte-identical to the previously-derived `expert_mask`, so
AITER paths (fp8/mxfp4/mxfp8/unquantized/quark) are behavior-unchanged.

**Perf** (DeepSeek-R1-0528-MXFP4, TP8 + `--enable-expert-parallel`, gfx950): an
earlier derive-based revision already showed no e2e regression (mean TPOT within
run noise, GPU-kernel time flat); this revision removes the derive entirely — the
AITER experts read the precomputed `expert_mask`, so the four tiny per-MoE-layer
kernels (fill/compare/cast/cat) are gone. Trace re-confirmation to follow.

Draft — AI assistance was used; the submitter is validating and iterating.

commits.pr_body:
[PR #50137](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50137) fixed fused per-channel scale loading, but shape-based orientation inference cannot reliably recover the checkpoint layout after both dimensions have been divided by the quantization block size. - Enable the transposed layout for Qwen3-VL MoE while preserving the decoder-layer override used by downstream models such as InternS1Pro.
- Transpose fused weights and canonical block scales, while leaving per-channel scales and other independently laid-out quantization metadata unchanged.
- Cover standard and transposed w1/w2 weights and scales, including rectangular and square block-scale layouts.

commits.pr_title: [CI] Restore MiniCPMV transformers cap, scoped to HF runner only
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Restores the `max_transformers_version` cap on the `MiniCPMV` test registry entry, scoped to the HF runner only (`transformers_version_reason={"hf": ...}`).

This PR previously flipped an existing `"vllm"` reason to `"hf"`. Since then #48413 removed the cap outright, so it has been rewritten: the cap is re-added, with the correct reason.

## Why the cap is needed again

Nightly [build 83094](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/83094) (`Multi-Modal Models (Extended Generation 3)`, an `optional: true` step that only runs in the scheduled full CI run) fails 9 tests, all with:

```
AttributeError: 'MiniCPMV' object has no attribute 'all_tied_weights_keys'
```

- `test_single_image_models[minicpmv_25-test_case100..102]`
- `test_single_image_models[minicpmv_26-test_case103..105]`
- `test_multi_image_models[minicpmv_26-test_case77..79]`

The failure is entirely on the HF reference side. The traceback ends in `transformers/modeling_utils.py`:

```python
for key in missing_keys - self.all_tied_weights_keys.keys()
```

`all_tied_weights_keys` is set by `PreTrainedModel.post_init()`, and MiniCPMV's remote code never calls it: `post_init` appears zero times in `modeling_minicpmv.py` for `MiniCPM-Llama3-V-2_5`, `MiniCPM-V-4` and `MiniCPM-V-4_5` (2_6 is gated on the Hub now, but fails identically). Same failure mode as `SkyworkR1VChatModel` (#42104) and the sibling `MiniCPMO` entry, both already capped.

### Why it surfaced now

The `MiniCPMV` entry used to carry `max_transformers_version="4.57"` with a `"vllm"` reason. Because `vlm_utils/core.py::run_test` calls `check_transformers_version(on_fail="skip")` with the default `check_max_version=True`, that cap gated the HF-runner tests too. #48413 fixed the vLLM-side `MiniCPMVBatchFeature` problem and removed the cap entirely, which correctly re-enabled vLLM-only coverage but also un-gated the HF comparisons and exposed this separate, still-unfixed HF-side break.

Using an `"hf"`-scoped reason keeps both halves right: HF-runner comparisons skip, vLLM-only tests (including the ones #48413 added in `tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_minicpmv.py`) keep running, because those callers pass `check_max_version=False, check_version_reason="vllm"`.

Tracks under #38379.

## Not a duplicate

This *is* the pre-existing PR for this fix, rewritten rather than superseded by a new one. Duplicate checks run:

```
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "minicpmv"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "all_tied_weights_keys in:body"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "48413 in:body"
```

No other open PR touches the `MiniCPMV` registry entry. #43760 and #42785 are runtime/CUDA-graph changes to the model itself.

## Testing

```
pytest tests/models/test_registry.py -q
```
